The clearest regularization control is [CL4SRec](https://arxiv.org/html/2010.14395), which compares random contiguous cropping, item masking and reordering, both as plain training augmentation and with contrastive loss. On Yelp, crop-only augmentation raises HR@20 from 0.0529 to 0.0576; masking raises it to 0.0546. These results show that context perturbation can help without preferentially retaining recent history. They do not establish a recency mechanism: matched recent-versus-old removal is absent. [RSS](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/299238/2/299238.pdf) provides complementary evidence for recency-weighted training-target sampling, but changes target selection rather than isolating context truncation.

For elapsed time, [TiCoSeRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08262) studies uneven interaction intervals and time-aware augmentation; it supports treating timestamps separately from interaction positions, but does not directly establish whether last-k events outperform a count-matched last-Δt horizon. For context mismatch, [Closing the Long-Short View Gap](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.06219) examines the reverse direction—long-history training followed by short-history inference. Restoring a few prefix tokens sharply improves performance, which the authors attribute partly to attention sinks; therefore, truncation losses need not measure lost historical preference information alone.

The requested complete factorial control was not located. A discriminating BERT4Rec experiment would match retained counts across recent suffixes, old prefixes, random subsets and random contiguous crops; preserve targets, masking, positions and training budget; and cross cropped/full training with cropped/full inference. Separately compare event-count and elapsed-time horizons while matching counts and stratifying activity rates. Recent-history superiority over equally short controls would support recency; comparable gains would support generic regularization. Cropped-training/full-inference performance must be measured directly rather than inferred from augmentation results.
